newsitem.title: USA: NYPA says has approval to set up transmission plan.
newsitem.headline: NYPA says has approval to set up transmission plan.

text.p: The New York Power Authority (NYPA) said Tuesday its trustees approved a plan under which it would help set up an Independent System Operator (ISO) for New York state's transmission system.

"(This) marks one of the first joint actions by utilities to open the state's transmission network to any power marketer," NYPA chairman and chief executive officer C.D. Rappleyea said in a statement.

Rappleyea said the ISO proposal was the result of two years of work with New York's Public Service Commission, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the state's seven investor-owned utilities and trade and environmental groups.
The plan, a key step toward opening the state's electricity industry to open competition, will be submitted to FERC January 31 for approval.
"If approved, (it) could be partially implemented in mid-1997, with full implementation anticipated by mid-1998," NYPA said.
FERC, which would regulate the ISO, last year ordered utilities nationwide to prepare a plan that would open their high-voltage lines to all bulk power marketers.

The NYPA plan approved by trustees would establish a not-for-profit ISO corporation replacing the existing New York Power Pool (NYPP), providing access and coordination functions for all users of the grid similar to those currently available from NYPP.
"Maintenance and basic operation of the system would remain the responsibility of the transmission owners," NYPA said.
ISO's functions would include balancing the grid's power load, dispatching electricity, and setting some pricing.
It would be governed by 28 representatives from transmission owners (8), wholesale power buyers (8), wholesale sellers (8), and environmental and consumer groups (4).
The plan also calls for a New York State Reliability Council, a voluntary association that would ensure operations comply with standards set by local and national regulators.
The council would consist of an 11-member board representing transmission owners (8) and one representative each of electricity sellers, buyers, environmental and consumer groups.

The plan calls for setting up a Power Exchange (PE) to meet power demand identified by the ISO. Transmission owners would establish one PE, but others could be established, with governance based on the level of participation in trade.
According to the statement, transmission prices would be based on "Locational Based Marginal Pricing," a mechanism for showing price differentials between various delivery points on the system.
Customers would also pay a transmission service charge to cover the fixed transmission costs of the local utility.
